claim: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology is conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012.
source: The Reproducibility Project: Cancer Biology seeks to address growing concerns about reproducibility in scientific research by conducting replications of 50 papers in the field of cancer biology published between 2010 and 2012.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a description of the project scope.

claim: Arthur et al. (2012) identified a genotoxic island in Escherichia coli NC101.
source: Arthur and colleagues identified a genotoxic island in Escherichia coli NC101 that appeared to be responsible for causing neoplastic lesions in inflammation-induced IL10−/− mice treated with azoxymethane.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and references the original Arthur et al. 2012 study.

claim: The genotoxic island in E. coli NC101 appeared to be responsible for causing neoplastic lesions in inflammation-induced IL10−/− mice treated with azoxymethane.
source: Arthur and colleagues identified a genotoxic island in Escherichia coli NC101 that appeared to be responsible for causing neoplastic lesions in inflammation-induced IL10−/− mice treated with azoxymethane.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and references findings from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: IL10−/− mice inoculated with a mutated strain of E. coli NC101 lacking the genotoxic island suffered from fewer neoplastic lesions than mice inoculated with wild type E. coli NC101.
source: Arthur and colleagues inoculated IL10−/− mice with a mutated strain of E. coli NC101 lacking the genotoxic island, and showed that those mice suffered from fewer neoplastic lesions than mice inoculated with the wild type form of E. coli NC101 (Figure 4).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the abstract and references Figure 4 from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: There was a shift in the composition of the microbiota in Il10−/− mice, which develop chronic colitis.
source: They identified a shift in the composition of the microbiota in Il10−/− mice, which develop chronic colitis
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: Escherichia coli was over 100-fold more represented in Il10−/− mice than wild type.
source: amongst other changes noted, Escherichia coli was over 100-fold more represented in Il10−/− mice than wild type.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: Germ-free Il10−/− mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101 and treated with azoxymethane developed invasive mucinous carcinomas.
source: After treatment with azoxymethane (AOM), a carcinogen that induces colon cancer, germ-free Il10−/− mice mono-associated with the colitis-inducing E. coli NC101 strain developed invasive mucinous carcinomas
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: Germ-free Il10−/− mice mono-associated with Enterococcus faecalis and treated with azoxymethane did not develop invasive mucinous carcinomas.
source: while mice mono-associated with Enterococcus faecalis, another colitis-inducing bacterial strain, did not.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: E. coli NC101 harbors a 54 kb polyketide synthases (pks) genotoxic island encoding several enzymes involved in the production of toxin called Colibactin.
source: E. coli NC101 harbors a 54 kb polyketide synthases (pks) genotoxic island encoding several enzymes involved in the production of toxin called Colibactin.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section.

claim: The pks genotoxic island induces DNA damage, double strand breaks and aneuploidy.
source: This island has been previously shown to induce DNA damage, double strand breaks and aneuploidy (Nougayrede, 2006; Cuevas-Ramos et al., 2010)
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and supported by citations to Nougayrede 2006 and Cuevas-Ramos et al. 2010.

claim: The pks genotoxic island was not found in E. faecalis or E. coli strain K12.
source: and was not found in E. faecalis or another non-colitic E. coli strain, K12.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section.

claim: Loss of the pks island did not impair bacterial growth of E. coli NC101.
source: Arthur and colleagues first confirmed that loss of the pks island did not impair bacterial growth (Supplemental figure 7, replicated in Protocol 1).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Supplemental figure 7 from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: Presence or absence of the genotoxic pks island had no effect on colonic inflammation in IL10−/− mice alone or treated with AOM.
source: Presence or absence of the genotoxic pks island had no effect on colonic inflammation in IL10−/− mice alone or treated with AOM (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Figure 4A from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: At 12 and 18 weeks, mice treated with AOM and inoculated with E. coli NC101Δpks had many fewer neoplastic lesions than mice inoculated with wild-type E. coli NC101.
source: However, at 12 and 18 weeks, mice treated with AOM and inoculated with E. coli NC101Δpks had many fewer neoplastic lesions than mice inoculated with wild-type E. coli NC101 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Figure 4B from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: At 18 weeks, invasion was reduced in mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101Δpks as compared to NC101.
source: At 18 weeks, invasion (Figure 4C), tumor burden (Figure 4D) and tumor size (Figure 4E) were all reduced in mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101Δpks as compared to NC101.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Figure 4C from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: At 18 weeks, tumor burden was reduced in mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101Δpks as compared to NC101.
source: At 18 weeks, invasion (Figure 4C), tumor burden (Figure 4D) and tumor size (Figure 4E) were all reduced in mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101Δpks as compared to NC101.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Figure 4D from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: At 18 weeks, tumor size was reduced in mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101Δpks as compared to NC101.
source: At 18 weeks, invasion (Figure 4C), tumor burden (Figure 4D) and tumor size (Figure 4E) were all reduced in mice mono-associated with E. coli NC101Δpks as compared to NC101.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Figure 4E from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: Loss of the pks genotoxic island from E. coli NC101 strongly reduces the incidence of colon cancer in mice with chronic colitis.
source: Taken together, the data indicate that loss of the pks genotoxic island from E. coli NC101 strongly reduces the incidence of colon cancer in mice with chronic colitis.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section as a summary of findings from Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: The genotoxic pks island is more prevalent in patients with colorectal cancer according to the dataset from Arthur et al. (2012).
source: Both the dataset from Arthur et al. (2012) and the dataset presented by Buc et al. (2013) support the hypothesis that the genotoxic pks island is more prevalent in patients with colorectal cancer.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Arthur et al. 2012.

claim: The genotoxic pks island is more prevalent in patients with colorectal cancer according to the dataset from Buc et al. (2013).
source: Both the dataset from Arthur et al. (2012) and the dataset presented by Buc et al. (2013) support the hypothesis that the genotoxic pks island is more prevalent in patients with colorectal cancer.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Buc et al. 2013.

claim: Cougnoux et al. (2014) extended the findings of Arthur and colleagues to explore the mechanism of pks-produced colobactin toxicity effects on colorectal cancer.
source: Cougnoux et al. (2014), while not performing a direct replication, extended the findings of Arthur and colleagues to explore the mechanism of pks-produced colobactin toxicity effects on colorectal cancer.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Cougnoux et al. 2014.

claim: Arthur et al. (2014) demonstrated that colon inflammation itself has an influence on the expression of the genotoxic pks island.
source: Finally, Arthur and colleagues have since published further work exploring in greater detail the genetic mechanisms behind the association of colorectal cancer with colitis and colonization by E. coli NC101 with or without the pks island, in which they demonstrate that colon inflammation itself has an influence on the expression of the genotoxic pks island (Arthur et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is directly stated in the Introduction section and references Arthur et al. 2014.

claim: The replication experiment will be repeated a total of three times for Protocol 1.
source: This experiment will be repeated a total of three times.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in Protocol 1 Sampling section.

claim: Power calculations were not performed for Protocol 1, as no significant difference was reported in the original study.
source: Power calculations were not performed, as no significant difference was reported in the original study.

claim: The expected survival rate for germ-free IL10−/− mice treated with AOM and inoculated with E. coli NC101 is 75%.
source: Expected survival is 75% (as seen in Supplemental figure 10), thus 14 mice are required to predict 10 will survive.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in Protocol 3 Sampling section and references Supplemental figure 10.

claim: The expected survival rate for germ-free IL10−/− mice treated with AOM and inoculated with E. coli NC101Δpks is 62.5%.
source: Expected survival is 62.5% (as seen in Supplemental figure 10), thus 16 mice are required to predict 10 will survive.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in Protocol 3 Sampling section and references Supplemental figure 10.

claim: Azoxymethane (AOM) can show lot-to-lot variation in potency.
source: Azoxymethane (AOM) can show lot-to-lot variation in potency, and will lose potency and gain toxicity over time.
evidence: This claim is directly stated in Protocol 3 Procedure Notes section.

claim: Azoxymethane (AOM) will lose potency and gain toxicity over time.
source: Azoxymethane (AOM) can show lot-to-lot variation in potency, and will lose potency and gain toxicity over time.

source: This experiment will use at least 10 mice per group for a final power of 80–96%.
